a.raw: we might be some good to her said matthew suddenly and unexpectedly
a.fixed: “We might be some good to her,” said Matthew suddenly and unexpectedly.
a.why: Matthew’s real words (Anne of Green Gables, Ch. 3): the comma goes inside the closing quotation mark, then the tag, then a period.

b.raw: anne and annemarie are both brave but they show it in different ways
b.fixed: Anne and Annemarie are both brave, but they show it in different ways.
b.why: Capitals on both names; a comma before but joins two complete thoughts; a period ends it.

notes.wgrd: Compare themes across texts: name a theme, find it in two books, and say how the characters show it alike and differently.
vocab: The big idea about life that a story keeps showing.
To tell how two things are alike.
To tell how two things are different.
Details from the text that prove what you say.
notes.wordParts: Every base from the year: port, tract, struct, spect, ject, script, rupt, duct, form, press, tain, lev, plus prefixes like pre-, re-, trans-, inter-.
notes.grammar: Spiral review: capitals, commas, quotation marks, complete sentences. Read your sentence out loud and check each mark has a job.
notes.spelling: Spiral review: drop the silent e, change y to i, double the last consonant when the beat is on the last syllable, and spell each word part the same way every time.

grammar.label: Opti · every mark has a job

transcripts.welcome: Hoo! It’s Opti. You chose a theme. Today you find it in two different books. Today’s question: how can two characters show the same idea in different ways?
transcripts.read: Pick two characters from two books who show your theme. Write one moment for each. Then ask: how are they alike, and how are they different? Think about what makes each one act.
transcripts.grammar: Every punctuation mark has a job. A capital starts a sentence and a name. A comma joins or separates. Quotation marks hold someone’s exact words. Read your sentence out loud, and ask each mark: what’s your job?
